Beállítom A rendőrség hivatalos tájékoztatása szerint tizenketten haltak meg vasárnap hajnalban, miután egy lengyel rendszámú busz éjjel 1 óra környékén felborult az M3-as autópálya Nyíregyháza felé vezető oldalán a mezőkeresztesi lehajtó után. A Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén Vármegyei Rendőr-főkapitányság a police.hu-n azt írta, jelenlegi adataik szerint feltehetőleg a sofőr elaludt, őt a rendőrök őrizetbe veszik. Janasóczki Attila rendőrségi szóvivő korábban az MTI-nek azt mondta, hogy a halálos áldozatok mellett a balesetben legalább tíz ember megsérült. Az érintett autópálya-szakaszt a helyszínelés és műszaki mentés idejére lezárták. A forgalmat Mezőkeresztesnél terelik le, Emődnél lehet visszatérni az autópályára. A katasztrófavédelem szerint ötvenhét utas és két sofőr ült a turistabuszon. Hajnali három órakor jelezték, hogy a tűzoltók addig harmincöt embert mentettek ki a buszból, és több utas a jármű alá került. A huszonnégy tonnás busz mozgatásához civil daruk is a helyszínre tartottak, amíg ezek megérkeztek, a tűzoltók próbálták a hátsó tengelyt annyira megemelni csörlőzéssel, hogy ki tudják emelni az alatta lévő embereket. A helyszínre melegedőbusz, valamint Lengyelországból egy mentesítő járat is elindult. Az Országos Mentőszolgálat (OMSZ) megerősítette, többen is életüket vesztették a balesetben. A tömeges baleseti protokollnak megfelelően számos mentőegységet riasztottak a helyszínre, a további sérültek ellátása és kórházba szállítása folyamatban van. A balesetről Magyar Péter is posztolt reggel a Facebookon, a miniszterelnök részvétet nyilvánított az áldozatok családjainak, és megköszönte a mentésben résztvevők munkáját. Photograph: Google Maps Tennessee US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition Angela Lipps, 50, alleges in suit that Fargo police wrongly relied on AI facial recognition to arrest and charge her Lucy Campbell Fri 18 Sep 2026 19.34 EDT Last modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 20.29 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Tennessee woman who was falsely charged with bank theft in North Dakota and jailed for six months has sued for $10m in damages, alleging in a federal lawsuit that Fargo police improperly relied on an artificial intelligence (AI) facial recognition system to wrongly accuse her. Angela Lipps, 50, was arrested at gunpoint by US marshals at her home in Tennessee while babysitting her neighbor’s four children in July 2025. The mother of three and grandmother of five was booked into a county jail and remained there for almost four months without bail while awaiting extradition to North Dakota , where she was held for about two more months. Lipps, who has lived most of her life in north-central Tennessee, had never been on a plane until authorities flew her to North Dakota at the end of October, where she was charged with four counts of unauthorized use of personal identifying information and four counts of theft. The charges were ultimately dropped, and she was “released into the freezing cold … on Christmas Eve with no way to get home” after her lawyer, Jay Greenwood, provided bank records proving that she was in Tennessee at the time the fraud occurred in Fargo, the complaint says. Another attorney for Lipps, Eric Rice, told Tennessee television station WKRN that the $10m his client is seeking is “obviously … a significant number, but it reflects the specific harm that happened to Angela”. “Can you imagine being taken away at gunpoint, held in detention, taken from your family?” Rice said. A Fargo government spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation. Lipps’s lawsuit names the city of Fargo and Lucas Heck, a city police detective identified in the complaint as having requested the arrest warrant for her, as the defendants. The plaintiff alleges that she “experienced traumatic conditions in the jails”. “She struggled with the fear of not knowing when she would be released or whether she would end up wrongly convicted and imprisoned for years,” the lawsuit continues. “She missed family birthdays. She spent her own birthday incarcerated, separated from her family. She missed holidays with her loved ones, including Thanksgiving and Christmas. While in custody, she was denied basic care, such as her medications and her dentures.” Lipps learned she had lost her residence, her car and her personal property once she was released from custody, her lawsuit states. The experience, it says, has left Lipps with “lasting hardships and trauma that might be managed but never erased”. The “Fargo police department (FPD) and its agents have refused to accept responsibility or apologize to Lipps despite multiple requests for them to do so”, the complaint says. The lawsuit says that it seeks to “repair what has been broken” over her false arrest and “seeks accountability” from the FPD. Lipps’s complaint recounts how a west Fargo police investigator used AI facial recognition software to identify bank fraud suspects. The software returned Lipps’s social media photo as a potential lead, which was provided to Heck. It alleges that the source of the facial recognition was a fake ID used by a female suspect who was captured in surveillance video footage. Lipps did not look like the female suspect and had also never been to North Dakota, according to the complaint. The complaint alleges that Heck falsely suggested that facial recognition systems had identified Lipps and did not conduct further investigation or find sufficient probable cause – but requested an arrest warrant anyway. Lipps maintains she was unlawfully arrested and imprisoned – as well as maliciously prosecuted – and that the FPD lacked policy, training and supervision of officers on the use of facial recognition technology. “They knew that AI facial recognition technology should not be used as the sole basis to extradite and charge a person,” Lipps’s complaint alleges. “Yet they ignored those issues and gave no care to the harm it would do to innocent people like Lipps. “As AI facial recognition technology becomes more accessible and widespread, Lipps hopes that her case will cause officers to use appropriate care and consider the harm their actions can have on those who are wrongly accused.” Lipps’s lawsuit further alleges: “FPD was aware that the lack of supervision of an officer using facial recognition in an investigation could result in the wrongful detention and prosecution of a subject. Despite knowledge of this risk, FPD refused to supervise its officers’ use of facial recognition technology in a criminal investigation.” Explore more on these topics Tennessee US policing North Dakota US justice system news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.dw.com/en/can-south-korea-an.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OALw Zelenskyy's POW revelation at the UN has caused a major rift with Seoul Image: Seth Wenig/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement South Korea 's ambassador to Kyiv returned to Seoul on Saturday, his recall the latest in a series of tit-for-tat actions that have severely strained bilateral ties. The sudden deterioration in their relationship can be traced back to September 23, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the United Nations General Assembly in New York that Ukraine had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea. The soldiers had been captured by Ukrainian forces in the Russian Kursk region in January 2025 as they fought alongside Russian troops . The South Korean government immediately expressed its anger at Zelenskyy's revelation , insisting that the two governments had reached an agreement to keep the transfer of the two men in mid-September a secret. Kyiv hit back, by saying that no confidentiality agreement had been in place, to which South Korea accused Ukraine of effectively lying and demanded an official explanation and an apology . Ukraine has attempted to smooth over what it has called a "diplomatic understanding," but stopped short of the public apology that was expected in Seoul. Then, reports emerged last week that a close adviser to Zelenskyy had said that more than 176,000 tons of diesel and other energy products were shipped to Russia from South Korean ports in July and August of this year, which would be a breach of international sanctions. The office of president Lee Jae Myung in Seoul denied the accusation, and two days later recalled its ambassador to Kyiv. Prisoner swap: From North to South Korea via Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What is behind Seoul's need for secrecy? There are several reasons why South Korea wanted to keep the POW transfer secret, Erwin Tan, a professor of international politics at Hankuk University, told DW. "The first was that revealing that the POWs had been repatriated to South Korea would result in Pyongyang retaliating against the families of the men for surrendering," Tan said. "Seoul also wanted to maintain a channel for communication with Pyongyang," Tan said. "This is a major consideration for the left-leaning wing of Korean politics, which includes President Lee and has historically favored seeking rapprochement with the North ." Kim Sang-woo, a former politician with the left-leaning South Korean Congress for New Politics and now a member of the board of the Kim Dae-jung Peace Foundation, agrees that the South Korean government wanted to avoid "friction" with the North. But Kim pointed out that it was always very likely that both Moscow and Pyongyang would find out about the transfer sooner or later and that Lee was being criticized in some quarters at home for appearing weak. "There is criticism that Lee's administration is effectively appeasing the North, that it has become too soft, and that is a very worrisome situation," Kim said. Yet he admits to being surprised at how quickly the issue escalated. "I think Lee was very angry that he was publicly being accused of lying about the agreement and it rapidly grew into a very messy confrontation," he said. Why Seoul wants an apology from Zelenskyy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Has Zelenskyy's approach backfired? While it is unclear why Zelenskyy used his high-profile UN speech to announce the repatriation of the two POWs, Kim believes it may have been a calculated move to win more support from Seoul. Kyiv could have carried out a prisoner swap with the Russians and won the freedom of some of its own men in return. But, Kim pointed out, Ukraine instead chose to accede to Seoul's request in the hope that South Korea would respond with additional financial and possibly even military support. That move appears to have backfired. Professor Tan anticipates that the two governments will continue to "vent steam" over the issue. "Given the high profile nature of the mutual accusations, both sides will probably engage in a mutual blame game for the immediate future, but I doubt that it will turn into a long-term case of mutual acrimony," he said. "I anticipate that after the furor has died down and the press is looking for the next new story, both sides will quietly resume contact on the basis of mutual pragmatism."
